text.title: llm-judge-rubric-evidence-first Core Rules
text.summary: Migrated testable rules for llm-judge-rubric-evidence-first. Verify and refine before relying on for production.

rule.statement: Every judge prompt must require structured JSON output with: per-criterion evidence (verbatim quote from candidate), per-criterion score on a fixed scale, per-criterion rationale, and a final weighted total — in that order.
rule.rationale: Forcing the judge to quote evidence BEFORE emitting a score binds the score to specific text, which is what raises Cronbach's alpha from ~0.45 (1-10 prompts) to ~0.85 across studies summarised by Adnan Masood (2024) and Langfuse's 2026 evaluation guide.

rule.statement: Run the judge prompt on the same candidate set 3-5 times with shuffled candidate order; compute Cronbach's alpha across runs. Reject the judge if alpha < 0.7.
rule.rationale: An unstable judge can never be a reliable eval signal. Stability is a precondition, not a nice-to-have, per Galileo's 2026 framework.

rule.statement: For pairwise judging, randomise candidate order per task AND run each pair twice with positions swapped; final verdict requires agreement across both orderings — disagreements count as ties.
rule.rationale: Direct measurement by Arize (2024-2026) shows position-swap reduces Order Bias by 60-90%; tie-on-disagree prevents the judge from breaking arbitrary ties as if they were meaningful. Calibrate the effort: the 2026 systematic evaluation across 5 judge models and 3 benchmarks measures position bias at only ≤0.04 — real, cheap to remove, and the SMALLEST of the four bias categories. Swap positions because it costs one extra call, not because it is where the error lives; see r6-style-bias-dominates for where it actually lives.

rule.statement: Normalise candidate length before judging: truncate to a common token cap, OR add explicit instruction "ignore length differences; longer is not better".
rule.rationale: Verbosity bias is consistently 10-30% on raw prompts (Arize 2026 LLM-judge writeup); normalisation drops it to under 5%. The direction is NOT uniform across model families and a single "longer is better" correction will therefore over-correct on some judges: measured, Gemini Pro / Flash / Llama favour longer output at +0.24 to +0.44, GPT-4o is near-neutral at −0.04, and Claude prefers concise at −0.12. Know your judge's sign before you normalise.

rule.statement: Normalise FORMATTING across candidates before judging — strip or equalise markdown, headings, bullet structure and emphasis — and state in the rubric that presentation is not a criterion. This normalisation is mandatory whenever the candidates were produced by different prompts, different models, or different post-processing, because those are exactly the conditions under which formatting differs systematically.
rule.rationale: Across 5 judge models, 3 benchmarks and a released 375-pair controlled dataset, style bias — a preference for markdown-formatted responses over equivalent plain prose — measures 0.10-0.76, up to 19x larger than position bias at ≤0.04. It is the dominant failure mode and the one most rubrics do not name. A judge whose style preference happens to match your house style is the dangerous case: it will over-reward your existing habits even where they lost information, and the agreement will read as validation.

rule.statement: Cross-judge: never use a single model family as the only judge for outputs from that same family. Use at least two different families (e.g., Claude judges GPT outputs, GPT judges Claude outputs) and compare.
rule.rationale: Self-preference is well-documented (Zheng et al. MT-bench, replicated across 2024-2026 evaluations). Cross-family judging exposes the bias and lets you flag tasks where only the in-family judge "agrees".

rule.statement: When criteria_count is above 5 AND bias_targets names all four bias classes (position, verbosity, self-preference, style), the judge-spec MUST split the rubric into multiple judge prompts of at most 5 criteria each, grouped by the kind of evidence they quote, with the per-judge weights fixed in the spec before any scoring, and each judge prompt MUST carry every mitigation: JSON output with evidence before score (r1); pairwise runs in both orders with disagreement counted as a tie (r3); length normalisation with the judge model's measured verbosity sign stated (r4); formatting equalised and presentation excluded as a criterion (r6-style-bias-dominates); judge_model from a different family than the system under test plus a second-family judge (r5); temperature 0 and a result cache keyed on judge, prompt hash and output hash (fm-02); and Cronbach's alpha at or above 0.7 per judge over 3-5 shuffled runs (r2).

rationale.source: Zheng et al., Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena (NeurIPS 2023); arXiv:2604.23178 (TMLR 2026)

rule.rationale: Past five criteria a single prompt drifts into a holistic impression and the per-criterion scores collapse toward one value (fm-01); splitting by evidence type keeps each score bound to a quote. Naming all four biases means each has its own mitigation and its own detector, since the measured magnitudes differ by an order of magnitude (style up to 0.76, position at most 0.04) and a single generic 'be unbiased' instruction addresses none of them.

rule.statement: When criteria_count is above 5 AND bias_targets is a subset of the four bias classes, the judge-spec MUST split the rubric into judges of at most 5 criteria each with fixed weights (as in r-advanced), apply exactly the mitigation matching each listed target (position -> r3, verbosity -> r4, self-preference -> r5, style -> r6-style-bias-dominates), and record every unlisted bias class as an accepted risk with a one-sentence reason. JSON evidence-first output (r1), temperature 0 with caching (fm-02) and the alpha at or above 0.7 stability gate (r2) remain mandatory on every judge.
rule.rationale: Every mitigation costs calls or preprocessing, so a spec should pay only for the biases it decided to target; what it must not do is leave the untargeted ones unnamed, because the largest measured bias (style) is the one most rubrics omit by default. The split-and-weight structure is what keeps the per-criterion scores interpretable when the criteria count is large.

rule.statement: When criteria_count is 5 or fewer, the judge-spec MUST use a single judge prompt: with one criterion, a focused prompt scoring pass / partial / fail with a verbatim evidence quote; with two to five, one per-criterion JSON block in the r1 order (evidence, score, rationale, weighted total) on a 1-3 or pass / partial / fail scale, never 1-10 (fm-01). Position swap (r3) is required whenever the judging is pairwise, the 'longer is not better' instruction (r4) is always present, temperature is 0 with caching (fm-02), and the stability run (r2) is still executed. Splitting into multiple judges is forbidden on this branch.

rationale.source: Zheng et al., Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena (NeurIPS 2023); Langfuse LLM-as-a-judge evaluation guide

rule.rationale: Up to five criteria fit one prompt without the holistic drift that forces a split, and a second judge would double cost for no gain in alpha. The coarse scale is deliberate: the 1-10 prompt is where scores cluster at 7, while a three-level scale with a quoted evidence line is what a second reviewer can actually verify.
